# Complete Knowledge Dossier: The Friends of Tunbridge Wells and Rusthall Commons

## Organization Identity
- Legal Entity: The Friends of Tunbridge Wells and Rusthall Commons
- Legal Status: Registered Charity in England and Wales
- Charity Registration Number: 1013975
- Founded: 1991
- Purpose: Protecting, preserving, enhancing, and securing community ownership of the 256 acres of common land known as Tunbridge Wells Common and Rusthall Common in Kent, UK.
- Governance Structure: Board of Trustees elected at the Annual General Meeting (AGM) by charity members.
- Official Website: https://friendsofthecommons.uk/
- Primary Contacts:
  - General Enquiries: info@friendsofthecommons.uk
  - Membership Enquiries: membership@friendsofthecommons.uk
  - Partnerships: partnerships@friendsofthecommons.uk
  - Ecology Reports: nature@friendsofthecommons.uk
  - Commons Ranger Office (Weekdays): 01892 554222
  - Duty Warden Mobile: 07887 655222
  - Police / Fire / Ambulance Emergency: 999

## Geography, Geology and Scale
- Total Protected Land: 256 acres (103.6 hectares) of unbuilt, unploughed common land.
  - Tunbridge Wells Common: 170 acres, located immediately adjacent to Royal Tunbridge Wells town centre and The Pantiles.
  - Rusthall Common: 86 acres, located to the north-west surrounding the village of Rusthall.
- Geology: Underlain by the Tunbridge Wells Sand Formation, part of the Lower Cretaceous Hastings Beds (approximately 135–140 million years old). Exposed rock formations comprise Ardingly Sandstone, characterized by honeycombed weathering, romantic holloways, and dramatic jointing.
- Key Formations:
  - Wellington Rocks (TN4 8HA): Celebrated sandstone outcrop on Tunbridge Wells Common, historic natural playground and viewpoint.
  - Toad Rock (TN4 8NX): Famous mushroom-shaped perched sandstone rock on Rusthall Common, celebrated by Victorian travelers.
  - Happy Valley & The 101 Steps: Steep sunken sandstone gorge connecting Mount Ephraim down to Tea Garden Lane and Rusthall.
  - The Roman Bank: Ancient earthwork embankment traversing Tunbridge Wells Common.
  - Queen Victoria Grove: Commemorative avenue of mature trees planted in 1897 to mark Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee.
  - Mill Pond and The Marlpit: Freshwater clay pits transformed into wildlife sanctuaries supporting breeding amphibians and waterfowl.

## Statutory Management and Byelaws
- Primary Legislation: Tunbridge Wells Improvement Act 1890.
- Managing Authority: Tunbridge Wells Commons Conservators (composed of representatives from the Freeholder, Tunbridge Wells Borough Council, and local ratepayers).
- Charity Role: The Friends work in active partnership with the Conservators, funding conservation projects, mobilizing community volunteers, and leading the campaign to acquire the freehold for the town.
- Core Byelaws & Visitor Code:
  1. No Open Fires or Barbecues: Strictly prohibited year-round due to high subsurface peat and dry gorse wildfire hazard.
  2. No Drones / UAVs: Prohibited by byelaw to safeguard wildlife, roosting pipistrelle bats, ground-nesting birds, and horse riders.
  3. Dog Walking Etiquette: Dogs warmly welcome under close control. Must be kept on short leads during ground-nesting bird season (March–July) and around sensitive wildlife ponds. 10+ red dog waste bins provided across entrances.
  4. Sandstone Preservation: Ardingly Sandstone is fragile. No carving graffiti, no climbing chalk, no chipping edges.
  5. Cycling: Restricted to designated surfaced bridleways and perimeter roadways; pedestrians and equestrians have strict right of way.
  6. Commercial Group Licenses: Groups of 4+ dogs and commercial fitness groups require a permit from the Commons Conservators.
- Parking Access (Open 24/7):
  - Tunbridge Wells Common (Fir Tree Road, TN4 8AH): Completely free, open 24/7, strictly restricted to max 4 hours stay.
  - Upper Pantiles / Major York's Road (Fairground Car Park, TN4 8HA): Open 24/7, pay-and-display parking.
  - Rusthall Common: Open 24/7, informal on-street parking on Coach Road, Common View, and Upper Street.

## Membership and Revenue Models
- Annual Individual Membership: £10 per year (provides 1 vote at the Charity's AGM and direct conservation funding).
- Annual Family / Household Membership: £20 per year (provides 2 votes at the Charity's AGM and direct household conservation funding).
- Payment Gateway: GoCardless Direct Debit (Individual ID: BRT00035S4J5CTW; Family ID: BRT0003629VSFKA).
- Direct Conservation Impacts:
  - £10: 20 metres of waymarked footpath signage.
  - £25: Stone drainage channel restoration around Wellington Rocks.
  - £50: Ultrasonic bat detector kits and woodland owl boxes.
  - £100: Emergency arboricultural care and storm bracing for 250-year-old veteran sweet chestnuts.

## The Historic Freehold Buyout Campaign
- Context: The historic freehold of the Commons has been held under the Manor of Rusthall since feudal times. It is currently held privately by property group Targetfollow.
- Campaign Objective: The Friends are leading a community-backed initiative to acquire the freehold, securing permanent civic ownership in a charitable trust forever.
- Community Support: Over 3,000 residents have formally pledged financial and civic support.
- Commercial Leverage Policy: The Charity maintains strategic confidentiality regarding total running pledge figures and acquisition targets to protect community negotiating strength with commercial counterparties.

## Local Tourism & Town Connections
- The Pantiles Georgian Colonnade (TN2 5TE): 200 metres from Lower Common; Georgian architecture, independent cafes, Chalybeate Spring, live open-air jazz.
- The Mount Edgcumbe (TN4 8BX): Historic 18th-century coaching inn built directly into the sandstone rock formations of the Common with cave cellars and terrace garden.
- Spa Valley Heritage Railway (TN2 5QY): Heritage steam and diesel trains operating from Tunbridge Wells West Station bordering the Common to High Rocks and Groombridge.
- The Toad Rock Retreat (TN4 8NX): Traditional dog-friendly village pub 100m from Toad Rock on Rusthall Common.
